title: Viking settlements
capsule: Viking expansion from Scandinavia, beginning with the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, established permanent settlements across the North Atlantic, the British Isles, Normandy, Kievan Rus, and as far as North America, where the L'Anse aux Meadows site in Newfoundland demonstrates a Norse presence around 1000 CE. In the British Isles, the Danelaw established by treaty in 886 gave Danish settlers legal control of eastern and northern England, while Norse colonies in Ireland produced towns including Dublin (c. 841), Waterford, and Limerick. Normans — descendants of Scandinavian settlers granted Normandy in 911 — conquered England in 1066, southern Italy and Sicily by 1071, and Antioch in 1098. Norse presence in the North Atlantic receded gradually after the thirteenth century as Greenland's Western Settlement was abandoned around 1350.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Viking settlements are attested through archaeology, sagas, and documentary sources, but as a polity entity this entry aggregates dispersed, non-unified settlements; territorial boundaries are inherently approximate and politically heterogeneous.
